problem.paragraph: Betty plans to invest a total of $$\text{\$12,000}$$ in mutual funds, certificates of deposit (CDs), and a high-yield savings account. Because of the risk involved in mutual funds, she wants to invest no more in mutual funds than the sum of her CDs and savings. She also wants the amount in savings to be at least half the amount in CDs. Her expected returns are $$11\%$$ on the mutual funds, $$8\%$$ on the CDs and $$6\%$$ on savings. How much money should Betty invest in each area in order to have the largest return on her investments? Set this up as a linear programming problem in the following form: Maximize $$\textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ subject to $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$$ . Do not find the solution.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 11–14, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) In a canonical linear programming problem, a nonnegative vector $$\textbf{x}$$ is a feasible solution if it satisfies $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ .

(T/F) If a canonical linear programming problem does not have an optimal solution, then either the objective function is not bounded on the feasible set $$\mathcal{F}$$ or $$\mathcal{F}$$ is the empty set.

(T/F) A vector $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ is an optimal solution of a canonical linear programming problem if $$f(\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}})$$ is equal to the maximum value of the linear functional $$f$$ on the feasible set $$\mathcal{F}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ is an optimal solution of a canonical linear programming problem, then $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ is an extreme point of the feasible set.

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 18–21 use the notion of a convex set, studied in Section 8.3. A set $$S$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is convex if, for each $$\mathbf{p}$$ and $$\mathbf{q}$$ in $$S$$ , the line segment between $$\mathbf{p}$$ and $$\mathbf{q}$$ lies in $$S$$ . [This line segment is the set of points of the form $$(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q}$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ .]

problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathcal{F}$$ be the feasible set of all solutions $$\mathbf{x}$$ of a linear programming problem $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ with $$\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$$ . Assume that $$\mathcal{F}$$ is nonempty. Show that $$\mathcal{F}$$ is a convex set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . [Hint: Consider points $$\mathbf{p}$$ and $$\mathbf{q}$$ in $$\mathcal{F}$$ and $$t$$ such that $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . Show that $$(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q}$$ is in $$\mathcal{F}$$ .]

Let $$\textbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ . The inequality $$ax_{1} + bx_{2} \leq c$$ for some real number $$c$$ may be written as $$\textbf{v}^{T}\textbf{x} \leq c$$ . The set $$S$$ of all $$\mathbf{x}$$ that satisfy this inequality is called a closed half-space of $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ . Show that $$S$$ is convex. [See the Hint for Exercise 18.]

The feasible set in Example 5 is the intersection of five closed half-spaces. By Exercise 19, these half-spaces are convex sets. Show that the intersection of any five convex sets $$S_{1}$$ , $$\ldots ,$$ ﻿ $$S_{5}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a convex set.

If $$c$$ is in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ and if $$f$$ is defined on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ by $$f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ , then $$f$$ is called a linear functional, and for any real number $$d$$ , $$\left\{ \textbf{x}:f\left( \textbf{x} \right) = d \right\}$$ is called a level set of $$f$$ . (See level sets in Figure 2 of Example 5.) Show that any such level set is convex.

list.item: The graph of the inequality consists of this line together with all points on one side of the line. To determine which side, pick a point not on the line to see if its coordinates satisfy the inequality. For example, try the origin, $$(0,0)$$ . The inequality $$- (0) + 2(0) \leq 8$$ is a true statement. Thus the origin and all other points below the line satisfy the inequality. As another example, substituting the coordinates of the point $$(0,8)$$ into the inequality produces a false statement: $$- (0) + 2(8) \leq 8$$ Thus $$(0,8)$$ and all other points above the line do not satisfy the inequality. Figure 7 shows small arrows beneath the graph of $$- x_{1} + 2x_{2} = 8$$ , to indicate which side is to be included.
